301.quote_or_event: According to Sikh tradition, Datu, the son of Guru Angad, resented that Amar Das had been made Guru in his place. He came to Goindwal, taunted Amar Das as a former water-carrier, and kicked him off his seat. Guru Amar Das did not retaliate. He humbly asked Datu's pardon, saying his foot must have been hurt, and then withdrew quietly to his home village.
301.explanation: Guru Amar Das was by then Guru with a following of his own, yet he answered a public insult and a physical assault with humility. Sikh tradition remembers the episode as a model of forbearance.
301.tie_back: The Kural says true restraint of anger is restraint where one has the power to act on it. Guru Amar Das held back his anger exactly where his position would have let it take effect.
301.source: Wikipedia, 'Guru Amar Das' (paraphrase of traditional accounts)
301._accuracy_note: A strong fit on restraint by one who could have retaliated. The source is Wikipedia, used as a last resort and summarising traditional Sikh accounts rather than contemporary records.

302.quote_or_event: “O anger, you are the root of conflict; compassion never rises up in you.”
302.explanation: In the Salok Sahaskriti, Guru Arjan addresses anger directly as the source of strife and as wholly without compassion. Anger (krodh) is one of the five thieves in Sikh teaching.
302.tie_back: The Kural says anger harms oneself when vented on the strong and is the worst evil when vented on the weak. Guru Arjan names what makes it so evil against the weak: it has no compassion.
302.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1358, Salok Sahaskriti, Guru Arjan (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
302._accuracy_note: Reasonable but partial: Gurbani condemns anger as merciless in every case and does not draw the Kural's distinction between anger against the stronger and the weaker.

303.quote_or_event: “Where there is greed, there is death. Where there is forgiveness, there is God Himself.”
303.explanation: In his saloks Bhagat Kabir sets forgiveness (khima) at the very centre of the spiritual life: where it is present, God is present.
303.tie_back: The Kural asks us to let go of anger toward anyone at all, because every evil is born of it. Kabir treats that letting go, forgiveness, as the place where God dwells.
303.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1372, Salok Bhagat Kabir (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
303._accuracy_note: A reasonable fit on releasing resentment through forgiveness. Kabir does not say that all evils spring from anger, and the verse is a Bhagat's saying in the Granth, not a Guru's.

304.quote_or_event: “Emotional attachment to Maya, sexual desire, anger and egotism are demons.”
304.explanation: In Raag Gujri, Guru Amar Das calls anger and the other passions demons that possess a person from within.
304.tie_back: The Kural asks whether there is any enemy greater than anger, which kills both the smile and the joy within. Guru Amar Das likewise counts anger among the inner demons that are a person's real foes.
304.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 513, Raag Gujri (Gujri ki Vaar), Guru Amar Das (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
304._accuracy_note: Next-best: the verse matches anger as the inner enemy but not the Kural's specific image of anger killing laughter and joy, and it groups anger with other passions.

305.quote_or_event: “Unfulfilled sexual desire and unresolved anger waste the body away,”
305.explanation: In the Dakhni Oankar Guru Nanak compares anger and lust to borax that melts gold: they consume the person who harbours them.
305.tie_back: The Kural warns that if you do not guard against anger, it will destroy you. Guru Nanak likewise describes anger wearing away the very one who keeps it.
305.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 932, Raag Raamkalee, Dakhni Oankar, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
305._accuracy_note: A strong fit on anger destroying its owner. The verse pairs anger with lust and speaks of physical wasting, while the Kural frames the point as self-protection.

306.quote_or_event: “The fire of anger is the outcaste who burns dead bodies at the crematorium.”
306.explanation: In Siree Raag Guru Nanak lists the inner outcastes that make a person impure. He names anger as a fire that burns as a cremation fire does.
306.tie_back: The Kural calls anger a fire that kills whoever comes near and burns up the raft of kin and friends. Guru Nanak shares the image of anger as a consuming, death-dealing fire.
306.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 15, Siree Raag, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
306._accuracy_note: Next-best: the fire metaphor matches, but Gurbani's point is inner impurity, and the Kural's image of a raft of kinsmen is absent. The caste language is used ironically to reject outward notions of impurity.

307.quote_or_event: “Fareed, do not turn around and strike those who strike you with their fists.”
307.explanation: In his saloks Sheikh Farid advises against answering blows with blows. He counsels humility instead of retaliation.
307.tie_back: The Kural says one who treats anger as useful will be hurt as surely as a hand that strikes the ground. Farid's advice not to strike back rejects anger as a tool of response.
307.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1378, Salok Sheikh Farid (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
307._accuracy_note: Next-best: both reject using anger as a means. Farid gives no image of self-injury and does not argue that anger rebounds on the angry person.

308.quote_or_event: Guru Arjan, the fifth Guru, was summoned by the Mughal emperor Jahangir and ordered to remove passages of the Adi Granth. He refused and was tortured to death at Lahore in 1606. Sikh tradition holds that he was made to sit on a red-hot iron plate while burning sand was poured over him. Through it he remained calm and without hatred, accepting God's will as sweet.
308.explanation: Guru Arjan is Sikhism's first martyr. His serenity under torture is remembered in Sikh tradition as the supreme example of bearing extreme injury without anger.
308.tie_back: The Kural says that even if someone does you harm like plunging you into a blazing fire, it is good to refrain from anger. Guru Arjan's martyrdom is almost a literal enactment of that teaching.
308.source: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'How did Guru Arjan die?' (paraphrase); hot-plate details from Sikh tradition
308._accuracy_note: A very close match in substance. Britannica confirms only the refusal and death by torture; the heated plate and hot sand are details from Sikh tradition.

309.quote_or_event: “Fareed, answer evil with goodness; do not fill your mind with anger. Your body shall not suffer from any disease, and you shall obtain everything.”
309.explanation: In his saloks Sheikh Farid tells the seeker to repay harm with good and keep anger out of the mind, promising wholeness and fulfilment in return.
309.tie_back: The Kural promises that one who never lets even the thought of anger into the mind will attain everything he sets his heart on. Farid makes the same promise in nearly the same terms.
309.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1381-1382, Salok Sheikh Farid (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
309._accuracy_note: A near one-to-one match: no anger in the mind, and everything is obtained. Farid adds returning good for evil, and the salok runs across the page break from Ang 1381 to 1382.

310.quote_or_event: “who is not touched by sexual desire or anger - within his heart, God dwells.”
310.explanation: In Raag Sorath, Guru Tegh Bahadur describes the person who stays even-minded in pleasure and pain, honour and dishonour. Because anger does not touch such a person, God abides in their heart.
310.tie_back: The Kural says those who have wholly given up anger are equal to those who have renounced the world. Guru Tegh Bahadur finds the true saint not in renunciation but in the one whom anger cannot touch.
310.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 633, Raag Sorath, Guru Tegh Bahadur (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
310._accuracy_note: A strong fit on freedom from anger as the mark of spiritual attainment. Sikhism rejects world-renunciation, so it agrees with the Kural's inner point but not with its praise of ascetics, and the Kural's first half, that the angry are like the dead, is not matched.
